lead: Image processing and computer vision both turn pictures into numbers and then into useful results. Image processing takes an image in and gives an image out: sharper, smaller, cleaner. Computer vision takes an image in and gives a description, count or decision: “cheque valid”, “lane clear”, “tumour present”. The same chain runs from a scene to a sensor to a digital image to a process to a decision. You meet it in hospital scans, satellite maps, OCR (optical character recognition), factory inspection, robots, security cameras, entertainment filters and QR or cheque scanning.

blocks.text: A digital image is a grid of numbers. Each element of the grid is a pixel, and the number stored at it is the brightness (intensity) of that pixel. A grayscale image stores one number per pixel; a colour image stores one number per channel, for example three numbers per pixel in RGB. Image processing changes those numbers and returns another image. Examples are contrast stretching of an X-ray, noise removal from a scanned form and compression of a photo. Computer vision uses the numbers to answer a question. It returns a label, a count, a position or an action. Reading a vehicle number plate and deciding whether a seat belt is worn are vision tasks.

The field grew from three pressures. Newspaper picture transmission needed pictures sent over long wires, so images had to be coded, sent and rebuilt. Medical imaging produced X-ray, ultrasound, CT (computed tomography) and MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) pictures that needed enhancement and measurement. Satellite imaging produced large images of land and weather. Factory inspection added a fourth pressure: fast, repeatable checks of manufactured parts.

The two names mark the output, not the difficulty. Some syllabi call the image-to-image side digital image processing and the decision side computer vision. Both need acquisition, storage and display. The chain is drawn below; acquisition details are in 1.4 and system blocks in 1.2.
Applications are best grouped by the decision they support. The table gives common domains and the output each one needs.

blocks.text: A shop payment flow shows the chain. A phone camera captures a QR code or cheque. Processing corrects skew, removes glare and binarizes the image. Vision decodes the QR payload or reads the cheque amount and account number. A decision then accepts the payment or sends the cheque for manual review. The task is a sequence of image operations followed by a decoder or classifier, not a single magic step.

The clean test is the output. If the output keeps the same pixel grid and only changes the brightness values (sharper, cleaner, smaller file), the task is image processing. If the output assigns a class, count, box, region label or action, the task is computer vision. A mask is a label map: one class label per pixel, not an improved copy of the input, so segmentation counts as vision. A system can contain both sides. A blur removal step is processing; the later character read is vision.

items: Write the input: image, video frame or sensor array.
Write the output: a changed image, a class, count, region label or action.
If the output keeps the same pixel grid and only changes brightness values, call it image processing.
If the output assigns a class, count, box, region label or action, call it computer vision.
Name the decision: accept/reject, class name, position or path.

blocks.where: W is image width in pixels, H is height in pixels, b is bits per pixel, and 8 converts bits to bytes. This is one uncompressed copy; multiply by the number of copies for total storage.

blocks.text: Use the same rule on exam questions. “Enhance a blurry cheque” is processing. “Read the cheque amount” is vision. “Compress an MRI” is processing. “Mark the tumour region” is segmentation: the output is a label map, one label per pixel, not a cleaner copy of the scan, so it is a vision step; see Unit 4. Recognition methods are in Unit 6.

examples.question: A shop scans a 1200×800 pixel cheque image at 8 bits per pixel. It stores three copies and sends them over a link. Find the size of one uncompressed copy in bytes and the total for three copies.
steps: Bits in one copy = 960,000 × 8 bits/pixel = 7,680,000 bits.
examples.answer: One uncompressed copy is 960,000 bytes (0.96 MB); three copies are 2,880,000 bytes (2.88 MB).
examples.check:
w = 1200
h = 800
bpp = 8
copies = 3
pixels = w * h
bits = pixels * bpp
one_bytes = bits // 8
one_mb = one_bytes / 1_000_000
total_bytes = one_bytes * copies
total_mb = total_bytes / 1_000_000
print(pixels)
print(bits)
print(one_bytes)
print(one_mb)
print(total_bytes)
print(total_mb)

traps: Do not call every task computer vision. If the output keeps the same pixel grid and only changes the brightness values, it is image processing.
Do not mix bits and bytes. A pixel at 8 bits needs one byte; a 24-bit RGB pixel needs three bytes before compression.
Do not mix decimal and binary megabytes. The example uses 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes; if a question uses 1 MB = 1,048,576 bytes, state it.
Do not think vision always means deep learning. Thresholding, edge detection and template matching are classical vision steps.
Do not forget that OCR, QR decoding and cheque reading contain both processing and vision parts.

quiz.q: Define image processing and computer vision by their outputs.
quiz.a: Image processing: image in, image out. Computer vision: image in, description, count or decision out.

quiz.q: Why did medical and satellite imaging help the field grow?
quiz.a: They produced large images that needed enhancement, compression and measurement. Medical work needs lesion detection; satellite work needs land, crop and flood maps.

quiz.q: A 640×480 grayscale image uses 8 bits per pixel. Find one uncompressed copy in bytes.
A system sharpens a blurred number plate, then reads the characters. Which part is processing and which is vision?
quiz.a: Sharpening returns an image, so it is processing. Reading returns text, so it is vision. The full system has both.

quiz.q: Name three application domains and one output for each.
quiz.a: Medical: lesion mask. Remote sensing: crop map. Document OCR: text. Inspection: pass/fail. Security: plate read.

quiz.q: Why digitize a scene before processing?
quiz.a: The sensor signal becomes numbers. Numbers can be stored, transmitted and changed by algorithms. Digitization uses sampling and quantization; see 1.6.

quiz.q: A shop scans a cheque, stores three copies and sends them. List two processing steps and one vision step before accepting it.
quiz.a: Processing: deskew and denoise, or binarize and compress. Vision: read the amount and account number. Decision: accept or refer. Storage uses the bytes formula.

beyond: Not for the exam. Embedded vision now runs on phone chips and camera modules, so QR decoding and cheque reading happen on the device. Medical imaging adds regulation and privacy to the accuracy problem. Remote sensing combines vision with weather and crop models. Search next for “image processing pipeline”, “OCR preprocessing”, “remote sensing classification” and “edge vision”. Foundation models are changing recognition, but the acquisition and image-processing chain still decides whether the input is usable.
